power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Mental disorders are typically approached as syndrome-defined states, and questions like why conditions outlast their triggers, why diagnoses overlap, why some resist treatment, how change occurs and what recovery should aim at are usually addressed separately.

Here, we approach mental health conditions as processes within a person's lifelong development, putting forward four propositions: 1) maintenance and development compete for a limited capacity for change; 2) repeated activity becomes structure; 3) self-maintenance can turn into entrapment, which depletes finite reserves; 4) reorganization is often abrupt and lasts only if consolidated.

From this perspective, mental health appears as the preserved capacity to keep developing, whereas many persistent conditions appear as active entrapment-a pattern reproduced by the person's own activity (avoidance, rumination).
Therefore, entering a state, remaining in it, leaving it and stabilizing the outcome can depend on different conditions.
For each of these phases we derive clinical implications and testable predictions.
Mental disorders affect more than one billion people, anxiety and depressive disorders being the most common (World Health Organization, 2025).
text.formatted: Mental disorders affect more than one billion people, anxiety and depressive disorders being the most common <ref type="bibr">(World Health Organization, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: There is an observed tendency for the early onset of these conditions: in a meta-analysis of 192 epidemiological studies, Solmi and colleagues (2022) placed the onset before age 14 in about a third of affected individuals, before age 18-in almost half, and before age 25-in more than 60%.

text.text: Despite this burden, treatment coverage remains low.

In the World Mental Health Surveys (21 countries), only 1 in 5 people with major depressive disorder in high-income countries, and 1 in 27 in low-and lower-middleincome countries, received minimally adequate treatment (Thornicroft et al., 2017).

text.text: Where treatment is delivered, its effects are real, although limited.

In an umbrella review of 102 meta-analyses (3,782 randomized controlled trials; ~650,000 adults with major mental disorders), Leichsenring and colleagues (2022) found pooled standardized mean differences of 0.34 for psychotherapies and 0.36 for pharmacotherapies against placebo or usual care, and concluded that these limited effects suggest a "ceiling effect" for treatment research as presently conducted.

text.text: Each of these approaches has advanced the field, although they have largely addressed different parts of the problem, and it remains unclear how are connected the key questions: 1) why conditions persist, 2) why they overlap, 3) why some resist treatment, 4) how change happens and 5) what recovery should aim at.
In our opinion, three reasons make these questions difficult to answer.
First, mental health conditions are processes that unfold over time, following the view set out by Nicholson and Dupré (2018) of living systems as constituted by processes instead of things.
text.formatted: First, mental health conditions are processes that unfold over time, following the view set out by <ref type="bibr">Nicholson and Dupré (2018)</ref> of living systems as constituted by processes instead of things.

text.text: However, most of the field's evidence comes from cross-sectional snapshots and group averages, which often fail to describe any single person (Fisher et al., 2018).
text.formatted: However, most of the field's evidence comes from cross-sectional snapshots and group averages, which often fail to describe any single person <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Fisher et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Second, a condition changes the person while the person lives with it and is treated for it, so the causes of its onset are not necessarily the causes of its persistence.
Third, a capacity on which many psychological treatments rely (the person's ability to observe/redirect their own mental activity) can itself be drawn into the condition.
Thus, the question should rather be how a developing system-the person-changes over time, and under which conditions it enters a state, remains in it and leaves it.
In the present work we propose a perspective that addresses these difficulties by treating each state as one phase of a process.

It is closest to three existing approaches (network and other dynamical-systems models, transdiagnostic and process-based approaches, and the cognitivebehavioral models describing the cycles that maintain particular disorders), and connects findings usually examined separately-by diagnosis, treatment modality and level of analysis, from synaptic plasticity to epidemiology.

To these approaches three distinctions are added: 1) entering a state, remaining in it, leaving it and stabilizing the new state are governed by different conditions; 2) resistance to treatment depends on which of the person's means of regulation (e.g., insight/motivation) the condition has captured, and on which reserves remain, indicating which interventions are likely to lose effect; and 3) change is more likely to last when, by the end of treatment, it is being built upon and transfers to other contexts, which offers a criterion for ending treatment and for anticipating relapse beyond symptom reduction.
As a result, a limited set of plausible and empirically testable predictions is obtained.
In this review we put forward four propositions on how mental health conditions change over time, and approach the five key questions raised above through this lens.
The four propositions and the reasons for choosing them are presented first (section 2).
The evidence on the five questions is then interpreted through these propositions (section 3).
Conditions outside the main pattern are considered separately (section 4), before the discussion of the clinical implications and tests of the proposal (section 5).
In this section we delimit what we understand by development in terms general enough to apply to mental life without reference to any particular model of a disorder.

By development of a system we understand its production of qualitatively new organization, which is further built upon, channeled through the constraints the system already has, conserved and integrated into a coherent whole.

In mental life, what develops is the person's organization of experience and action, hereinafter referred to as mental organization: the ways of perceiving, interpreting, feeling, acting and relating, each built on earlier ones and integrated into a coherent self.

This definition follows a long tradition in developmental science, from Heinz Werner (1890 Werner ( -1964)), for whom development combines differentiation with integration (Werner, 1957), to Jean Piaget (1896 -1980), for whom it combines the revision of existing structures with their preservation (Piaget, 1975 (Piaget, /1985).

text.text: Werner's differentiation and integration correspond to the production of new organization and its integration into a whole, whereas Piaget's revision and preservation correspond to its channeling through, and conservation within, the structures that already exist.

Seen from outside, development of a person's mental organization can be recognized by four markers: 1) new ways of understanding or acting appear; 2) later changes build on earlier ones; 3) what is new transfers to other relevant contexts; and 4) it persists after the intervention that produced it is withdrawn, within the person's ordinary environment.
These markers describe the structure of a change, and not its value or direction.
The first three can be assessed when the change occurs, whereas the fourth can only be identified a posteriori.

They correspond to criteria already used to distinguish cumulative from isolated change (marker 2; Masten & Cicchetti, 2010), transferable from context-bound change (marker 3; Barnett & Ceci, 2002) and -in the terms of Soderstrom and Bjork (2015)-durable learning from momentary performance (marker 4).

text.text: Here we present four propositions that describe how a developing system changes over time (as a process), and apply them to mental health conditions.
Proposition 1.
Processes of maintenance and development compete.
A developing system must keep itself coherent and also produce new organization.
Both processes draw on the same limited capacity to modify itself.
If maintenance absorbs that capacity, the system persists without developing.
Conversely, if generation outruns maintenance, so that change comes faster than it can be assimilated, the system changes but loses coherence.
Proposition 2.
Activity internalizes, becoming structure.
What a self-modifying system repeatedly does is laid down (is internalized) as structure that then shapes its further activity.
The conditions under which a pattern arises are therefore not necessarily the conditions that keep it in place.
Proposition 3.
Entrapment is the price of self-maintenance.

A system that maintains itself through its own activity can become entrapped: the activity that maintains it reproduces the constraints that confine it, consuming resources without producing anything new.
The reserves that allow such a system to sustain periods of entrapment are finite.
Proposition 4.
Reorganization is discontinuous and must be consolidated.
Change accumulates within an existing organization until the latter is reorganized, often abruptly.
The new organization persists only if it is integrated with the rest of the system, and earlier organization is overlaid rather than erased.

Applied to a broad class of persistent conditions, the four propositions describe a single course: a pattern is laid down by the person's own activity (Proposition 2) into a "loop" that maintains itself while consuming reserves (Proposition 3) and the capacity for change required for development (Proposition 1), until a reorganization occurs that lasts only if it is consolidated (Proposition 4).

The five key questions raised above (why a condition persists, why it takes similar forms across diagnoses, why it resists treatment, how it changes and what makes the change last) address different parts of this course.
The propositions above were chosen because they meet three criteria.
The first is convergence: each is consistent with findings from at least two research traditions that use different methods and developed largely independently of one another (Table 1).

text.text: The second is necessity: each is needed to answer at least one of the questions raised above, and none restates another.
The third is joint productivity: together they yield predictions that none of them yields alone.

We intentionally left out propositions about specific mechanisms, whether genetic, neural or cognitive, as the propositions presented here concern how change is organized over time and are, thus, compatible with mechanistic accounts at any level.
Taken together, Propositions 2 and 4 lead to a corollary that runs through the rest of this article.

Just as the conditions that bring a state about are not necessarily those that keep it in place (Proposition 2), the conditions that allow a person to leave a state are not necessarily those that make what replaces it last (Proposition 4).
Entering a state, remaining in it, leaving it and stabilizing its successor are, thus, four phases, each governed by its own conditions (Figure 1).

text.text: Both distinctions already treat the course of a condition as a sequence of phases, although these are defined mainly by clinical features (symptom level, duration and recurrence), and not by what governs each of them.
With development understood in this way, we propose to regard mental health as the preserved capacity to keep developing while remaining coherent (Proposition 1).

Mental health is then neither the absence of disorder nor a state to be restored, but a capacity that can be preserved in some areas of a person's life (work, relationships, etc.) while being lost in others.

text.text: Many mental health conditions persist long after the events that triggered them have gone.

Recurrences can be less tied to external events than first episodes, as Kendler and coworkers (2000) found in a large cohort of women, in whom the association between stressful life events and the onset of major depressive disorder weakened as previous episodes accumulated, up to a threshold.

text.text: In other words, with each episode the condition depended less on what triggered it and more on its own history.
For the sake of fairness, it should be noted that this "kindling" pattern is still debated (Monroe & Harkness, 2005).

text.text: Etiological research has often focused primarily on causes of onset, encouraging the assumption that the conditions that started a disorder also sustain it.

Cognitive-behavioral research, by contrast, has identified maintaining processes, of which safety behaviors are probably the clearest example: they prevent feared outcomes from ever being disconfirmed (Clark, 1999), so that a person with panic disorder who holds on to something whenever they feel faint never learns that they would not have collapsed.

text.text: Repetitive negative thinking, such as worry and rumination (Watkins, 2008), and stress generation, in which the condition itself produces new stressful events (Hammen, 2006), play similar maintaining roles, and network models likewise describe disorders as self-sustaining states (Borsboom, 2017).

text.text: Put in the terms of Propositions 2 and 3, these findings share one structure: the person is not passive.

The mind remains active (checking, worrying, ruminating, avoiding, planning around the problem), but each cycle lays down the associations, habits and avoidances -a "selfconstructed niche"-that make the next cycle more likely.
By "activity" we understand here the ongoing operation of the person's mental organization, which implies neither choice nor fault.
This configuration, which we denominate active entrapment, is that of a mind that keeps working, but whose work rebuilds the pattern instead of moving beyond it.
Two features usually accompany it: the pattern is local, so other areas of life may still be developing, and the person often keeps a position from which the pattern is recognized as unwanted.
Activity alone, however, does not decide the outcome.
As Watkins (2008) concluded, repetitive thinking aids recovery when it is concrete and oriented to solving problems, but can maintain depression and anxiety when it is abstract and evaluative.

text.text: The same activity can, thus, either move the person beyond the pattern or rebuild it.
We refer to entrapment when the pattern is held mainly by what the person's own activity has laid down.

Nevertheless, such a loop can extend beyond the affected person when others take part in it, as in family accommodation of obsessive-compulsive symptoms (relatives taking part in rituals or adjusting family routines to them), which is associated with greater symptom severity (Wu et al., 2016).

text.text: Conversely, if a pattern is held mainly by current external conditions (ongoing threat, coercion, poverty, chronic pain and others), its persistence is possibly an adequate response to them, and not entrapment.

Thus, case formulation should address what maintains the condition at present, and not only what started it, including what the condition itself has laid down (=its "niche"): avoided places/people, abandoned roles/routines, disturbed sleep and newly generated stressors (Clark, 1999; Hammen, 2006; Salkovskis et al., 1999; Watkins, 2008).

text.text: Treatment can then build on the two features described earlier-the "observing position" that the person often preserves and the areas of life that continue to develop.

These correspond, respectively, to the capacity to shift perspective that Kashdan and Rottenberg (2010) place within psychological flexibility and to the connectedness, identity and meaning that people describe in personal recovery (Leamy et al., 2011).

text.text: Comparable cycles have been described, each in its own terms, in other diagnostic groups.

In posttraumatic stress disorder, thought suppression, rumination and safety behaviors prevent change in the trauma memory and in its appraisals, so that a sense of current threat persists (Ehlers & Clark, 2000).

text.text: We propose that active entrapment is a common maintaining structure of a broad class of persistent conditions, including anxiety disorders; obsessive-compulsive and related disorders; depressive disorders; trauma-and stressor-related disorders; substance-related and addictive disorders; and feeding and eating disorders-and not only of the processes in which it has been demonstrated.
If so, it can be expected that interventions chosen from a formulation of the maintaining loop, independently of diagnosis, outperform those chosen by diagnosis.

If diagnoses corresponded to separate diseases, the pervasive comorbidity between them (Plana-Ripoll et al., 2019) and the extreme heterogeneity within a single diagnosis (Fried & Nesse, 2015) would be anomalies.

text.text: One of the reasons lies in the prevailing classifications (the DSM and the ICD), which are primarily syndromic and define disorders by patterns of symptoms and signs, together with requirements for duration, distress or impairment and exclusions, and not by the processes that maintain them (Insel et al., 2010).

text.text: Dimensional and transdiagnostic approaches have addressed this difficulty.

In a randomized trial, the Unified Protocol -a single transdiagnostic treatment-proved equivalent to disorder-specific protocols for several anxiety disorders, with fewer patients dropping out (Barlow et al., 2017).

text.text: Active entrapment is a structure, and a structure can carry many contents, as the same kind of loop can run on bodily sensations, threats, intrusive thoughts, memories, substances, food or self-image (roughly, the contents of panic, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive, posttraumatic, addictive and eating disorders), and at different levels of organization (bodily, affective, cognitive, relational or identity-related).

Within this class of conditions, much of what distinguishes one diagnosis from another possibly lies in the content and the level on which the loop runs, although diagnostic categories also differ in time course, impairment, associated features and exclusion criteria.
In other words, different diagnoses can represent different realizations (=instances) of a shared structure.

A shared structure, thus, offers one possible explanation of why conditions co-occur, why a person may move between diagnoses over time (in a birth cohort followed for four decades, mental disorder life histories shifted among different successive disorders; Caspi et al., 2020), and why treatments aimed at the structure work across diagnoses.

text.text: We should note that this explanation is compatible with others, such as a liability shared across disorders, the so-called p factor (Caspi et al., 2014), partly genetic in origin (Cross-Disorder Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, 2019), and direct interactions between symptoms (Borsboom, 2017).

text.text: In this account, culture shapes the content of distress and the idiom in which it is expressed more than the structure itself.

Somatic symptoms, for example, can function as "idioms of distress" in many cultural groups, as documented by Kirmayer (2001), so that distress that elsewhere would be reported as sadness or worry is expressed through bodily complaints.

text.text: Moreover, in a meta-analysis of 45 studies, cultural concepts of distress were consistently associated with general psychological distress, whereas their associations with specific diagnoses (anxiety, depression, posttraumatic stress disorder, somatization) varied widely (Kohrt et al., 2014), as expected if such concepts name a distress shared across diagnoses instead of corresponding to particular ones.

text.text: The structural interpretation also loosens the categorical-versus-dimensional debate: which loop runs, and at which level, is a qualitative question, whereas how strong the loop is and how long it lasts are quantitative ones.
Clinically, it seems useful to record the structure of a condition alongside its diagnosis: which loop runs, on what content and at which level, what maintains it, and which reserves remain.
A person may, thus, need the same "structural work" under successive diagnoses-a continuity that the sequence of diagnostic labels does not reveal.

Culturally-specific presentations can likewise be read as idioms that may carry a familiar structure, so that treatment can be delivered through the person's own interpretive categories and social resources.
That shared treatments can work across diagnoses is established, at least for anxiety and depression (Barlow et al., 2017; Newby et al., 2015; Rahman et al., 2016).

text.text: Whether "structural assessment" can be transferred across cultures is less certain.

If culture shapes the content of a condition more than its structure, structural assessment could prove more transferable than syndrome-based diagnosis, a possibility that, to our knowledge, has not yet been tested.
Some conditions respond within weeks, whereas others resist years of treatment.

Illness severity and duration account for part of this difference, but cannot explain why a person with specific phobia typically experiences the symptoms as unwanted and seeks relief, whereas some people with anorexia nervosa consider aspects of the illness as valued-an ego-syntonic quality that can reduce their motivation for treatment and their engagement in it (Gregertsen et al., 2017).

text.text: Then, what makes a condition resist treatment beyond its severity?

text.text: What matters, thus, is not only how severe a condition is, but also which functions it has affected.
Early intervention, in turn, seeks to shorten the duration of untreated illness, which is associated with poorer outcomes in several conditions.

text.text: Important for the subject of this section, the route through which psychotherapy produces change also differs between patients.

In 608 outpatients, Gómez Penedo and colleagues (2023) estimated how strongly each patient's improvement followed sessions that brought mastery experiences (coping better with the problem) or clarification experiences (understanding it better): these links varied between patients and were only weakly predictable from baseline characteristics (r = .18 and .16, respectively).
The same treatment, thus, works through different routes in different patients, and which route will work cannot be anticipated reliably.

Two factors, or a combination of both, could underlie these differences: 1) the loss of the person's independent means of regulating the maintaining process, here termed capture, and 2) the depletion of the person's reserves.
Below, we analyze each of these possibilities.
Many psychological interventions depend, to varying degrees, on the means of regulation, so that the more of them the loop "absorbs", the less effective those interventions probably become.

Capture is a profile rather than a single degree-as insight, motivation, attention, behavioral control and identity can each be captured separately, and these channels overlap with the psychological dimensions of the extended evolutionary meta-model used in process-based therapy (S. C. Hayes et al., 2020).

text.text: Curiously, the channels can also diverge-a person may recognize a compulsion as senseless and still be unable to stop it, or lack insight and still respond to a behavioral intervention.
Conditions differ in their typical profiles, from patterns experienced as alien (ego-dystonic) to patterns that have become part of identity (ego-syntonic).
The second factor is depletion (Proposition 3).

Remaining entrapped consumes the person's reserves without replenishing them, in line with Hobfoll's (1989) view of stress as the loss of valued resources and with the cumulative physiological cost of stress known as allostatic load (McEwen, 1998)-two accounts in which the cost of sustained coping accumulates instead of being repaid.

text.text: These reserves can be of several kinds: physiological (sleep, nutrition, health), cognitive (attention, memory), motivational (interest, hope), social (support, roles) and material (income, housing).

Importantly, they are not interchangeable, so that a person with several independent reserves may sustain entrapment longer and leave it more easily, than one whose remaining functions depend on a single depleted resource.

For social reserves, an influence on the course of a condition is already documented: in a systematic review of 34 longitudinal studies, poorer perceived social support predicted more severe symptoms, poorer recovery and worse functioning in depression, with preliminary evidence for other conditions (Wang et al., 2018).

text.text: A similar notion has been developed in neurology, where cognitive reserve explains why some people tolerate more age-related or Alzheimer's pathology than others before their functioning declines (Stern, 2012).

text.text: Both factors can also act together, as apparently occurs in anorexia nervosa, where the valuing of the disorder combines with physiological depletion.
For the clinician, the profile of capture would then matter as much as overall severity, and it could be assessed channel by channel.

Where a channel is captured, interventions that do not depend on it can be given more weight (including those acting through the body, relationships or the environment, and pharmacotherapy when indicated), while rebuilding the captured channel becomes a treatment goal in itself.
Reserves can likewise be assessed by kind, and protected and restored from the start of treatment (Hobfoll, 1989; McEwen, 1998), which gives early intervention a further rationale.

Of note, perceived entrapment is not specific to suicidality: in a meta-analysis by Siddaway and colleagues (2015), perceptions of defeat and entrapment were strongly associated with depression, anxiety, posttraumatic stress disorder and suicidality alike-possibly the experienced side of the structure described here.

text.text: We propose that the channels of capture are separable, and that capture of a given channel reduces the response to interventions relying on that channel more than the response to interventions entering elsewhere.
A compelling test should compare both kinds of intervention in patients with and without capture of that channel.

We also propose that reserves measured before onset predict how long an episode lasts more than whether it begins, and that the number of independent reserves predicts duration at least as well as their total.

text.text: In psychotherapy, two such signals have been studied.
The first is instability-a rise in the irregularity of the fluctuations in patients' daily self-ratings.

These findings fit the network destabilization and transition model of A. M. Hayes and Andrews (2020), in which change proceeds in two steps: the entrenched pattern that maintains a problem (in the terms of section 3.1, the self-maintaining loop) is first destabilized, which shows as increased fluctuation of symptoms and emotions, and a more functional pattern can then emerge and stabilize.
How, then, can interventions as different as exposure, medication or a change of environment lead to similar outcomes?
We propose that any intervention can be described by three independent properties (Table 2).

text.text: The first is where the intervention enters (its site): at the level of the entrapment pattern, at a lower (physiological) level, at a higher (interpersonal or social) level such as relationships and roles, or through the environment.

The second is what it does to the pattern (its operation): it can loosen the pattern's constraints, as in exposure, where, according to the inhibitory learning account, new learning overrides the old fear associations without erasing them (Craske et al., 2014).

text.text: It can change what the pattern's elements mean, as in cognitive restructuring; or it can change the repertoire of elements, adding activities, relationships and contexts, or removing those that sustain the pattern.

The third is how the intervention is applied over time (its time regime): as a single acute intervention, as small changes that accumulate until the organization shifts (Proposition 4), or as a sustained condition.
As the "exit" is apparently not the easiest path from inside the pattern, entering from a site that is not itself entrapped may make change possible.

For example, combining psychotherapy, which enters at the level of the pattern, with pharmacotherapy, which enters at a lower (physiological) level, outperforms either alone in adult depression (Cuijpers et al., 2020).

Symptomatic remission and the recovery of a satisfying life often diverge.

As proposed in section 2.3, mental health is the preserved capacity to keep developing, and not a state to be restored.
This proposal has three consequences.
First, recovery runs forward: a developing system cannot return to a previous state, because what it has lived through has become part of its structure (Proposition 2).
The realistic aim is, thus, a new organization that integrates the experience, with the markers of development serving as indicators of whether such an organization has formed.
Second, activity is not development, as each of the functions that make up development can "run idle" (examples in Table 3).

text.text: Third, two different processes can follow the reduction/end of treatment.
If treatment suppressed the pattern without reorganizing it and the pattern returns when treatment is reduced or stopped-this corresponds to relapse.
If the body has adapted physiologically to the medication, so that reducing or stopping it destabilizes the body whatever the course of the original condition-it corresponds to withdrawal.
The two processes can co-occur, and withdrawal, being itself a destabilization, can precipitate relapse where no reorganization has taken place.
In psychological treatment, the equivalent of reorganization is what remains when the therapist is no longer accompanying the patient.

Treatment goals could then be framed as "resumed development," that is, in terms of what the person can do, relate to, learn and become, and not only as symptom thresholds or as a return to "how I was" (Huber et al., 2011; Leamy et al., 2011).

text.text: Taken together, this evidence allows us to propose a preliminary scheme of the course of persistent conditions (Figure 1): 1) the person's own activity lays down a pattern that closes into a self-maintaining loop (Propositions 2 and 3); 2) the loop consumes reserves and the capacity for change that development requires (Propositions 1 and 3); 3) the more of the person's means of regulation it captures, the harder the state becomes to leave; and 4) a reorganization, often abrupt, lasts only if consolidated (Proposition 4).

text.text: These steps might be interdependent.
In this scheme, the five questions share a common answer, but what remains uncertain is the trigger that sets the direction of reorganization once a state has been destabilized.
Not all mental health conditions follow the pattern of active entrapment, and in some of them the difficulty apparently lies elsewhere than in a loop that keeps rebuilding itself.
Below, we give examples of how such conditions might be described in terms of the propositions, and of how the aims of treatment would then differ.
A detailed analysis of each of them is out of the scope of the present work.
In psychotic disorders, the problem would lie (at least in part) in the relations between levels of organization.

A hallucination would then be less an excess of internally generated experience than a failure to keep what is generated answerable to sensory evidence, a view that coincides with accounts in which hallucinations arise when prior expectations outweigh sensory input, such as that of Corlett and colleagues (2019).

During a manic episode, generation would outpace integration-the second case described in Proposition 1.
This view is consistent with accounts of mania as a dysregulation of the reward and goal system, in which goal attainment can trigger an escalating pursuit of new goals (Johnson et al., 2012).

Here a natural question arises: how large is the share of cases that do not follow the proposed pattern?
A rough estimate can be obtained from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023, which did not count substance use disorders and dementias among mental disorders.

According to this study, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and neurodevelopmental conditions accounted for about one in five prevalent cases of mental disorders and a quarter of the disability-adjusted life years due to them, whereas the conditions proposed to follow the pattern (the main subject of this proposal-anxiety, depressive and eating disorders) accounted for about two-thirds of both (GBD 2023 Mental Disorder Collaborators, 2026).
It seems reasonable to ask what would follow if the proposed interpretation were carried into clinical practice.

text.text: Like the three axes of intervention, they do not amount to a new therapy, and what would change is how existing interventions are chosen, combined, timed and evaluated.
First, assessment would add to the diagnosis a formulation of what maintains the condition (the loop, its content and level, the channels it has captured and the reserves that remain).
Second, treatment would be selected and combined from that formulation, leading with interventions that do not depend on a captured channel, and gains consolidated before treatment ends.

Third, relapse risk would be judged not only by residual symptoms, but also by whether gains show the first three markers of development, which the proposal expects to predict relapse beyond symptom reduction (Table 5, prediction 8).

text.text: The present work has three main limitations.
First, the evidence reviewed here was selected to examine the propositions instead of being gathered systematically, and is mostly positive.
We conducted a brief, non-systematic search of the published literature for evidence that would meet any of the refutation criteria presented and found none.
The studies that come closest were not designed around the constructs proposed here, so the presented predictions remain open to test.
Second, the constructs introduced in the present work (active entrapment, capture, reserves and others) have not yet been operationalized.

Third, as the present work is theoretical, no participants were recruited and no demographic data (racial or ethnic identification, cultural or geographic background, sex or gender, and income, education or socioeconomic status) were collected.

The evidence we draw on comes from samples of different backgrounds, including surveys in 21 countries of different income levels (Thornicroft et al., 2017), a trial in a conflict-affected area of Pakistan (Rahman et al., 2016), studies of how distress is expressed in different cultural groups (Kirmayer, 2001; Kohrt et al., 2014) and a cohort of women (Kendler et al., 2000).

Mental health conditions are currently defined mostly by syndromes, studied crosssectionally and treated with symptom reduction as the main criterion of success.

The main difference of our proposal is that it approaches them as phases of a developmental process, addressing the three difficulties identified at the outset: the four phases treat conditions as processes (Figure 1), Proposition 2 accounts for the way a condition changes the person who has it, and capture describes how a condition absorbs a capacity on which many psychological treatments rely.

text.text: Why should a developing mind be prone to entrapment at all?

Within the proposal, the answer is given by Proposition 3: a system that maintains itself through its own activity cannot exclude that this activity reproduces the constraints that confine it: entrapment can become the other face of self-maintenance.
Recovery, in turn, runs forward toward a new organization and not back to a previous state (Proposition 2).

For practice, attention moves from the diagnostic label to what currently maintains a condition, from symptom reduction alone to whether change has become part of the person's organization, and from the end of an episode to the stabilization of what replaces it (Table 4).
